title: Long-Term MRR Investment Planning for Water Distribution Networks: A Risk-Weighted, Data-Driven Framework
content: Most North American drinking watermains were installed in the 1940s–1960s. A large share of these mains are well past their expected service life, with cast iron disproportionately driving the break rates. Most existing lifecycle costing frameworks, whether deterioration-based asset management models or standard MRR (Maintenance, Rehabilitation, and Replacement) cost tools, are tied to a fixed data level i.e., they are designed for data-rich utilities requiring asset and cost details most smaller utilities rarely hold. Additionally, many existing frameworks omit the effect of discounting which in turn obscures the NPV (Net Present Value) of future expenditure. This paper presents a data-tiered lifecycle cost framework, incorporating power-law non-homogeneous Poisson process break-rate modelling, risk-weighted prioritization, basic and advanced cost-assessment modules, and NPV discounting, to test whether proactive renewal strategies produce lower lifecycle costs than a fix-upon-break approach over 100 years and at what discount rate that advantage disappears. Applied to Kitchener (936 km) and Calgary (5,391 km), lining-heavy proactive strategies lower lifecycle cost by up to 12% and 20% at a 0% discount rate. The savings become negligible near 3% discount rate and reverse above it. Utilities can therefore run the framework on inventory and break records alone and establish whether proactive renewal remains defensible at their own discount rate.
